rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In long passages, stories, parenthetical clauses, and recitations combining readings, pauses may be licensed where they would otherwise be disallowed; al-Sajawandi calls this necessity-licensed stopping.
rows.anchor: يغتفر في طول الفواصل والقصص والجمل المعترضة ونحو ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن الجزري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jazari prefers examples such as the paired directions, prophets, prayer and almsgiving, and the story endings in al-Muʾminun for necessity-licensed stopping.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الجزري والأحسن تمثيله بنحو ﴿ قبل المشرق والمغرب ﴾ وبنحو ﴿ النبيين ﴾

rows.speaker: صاحب المستوفى
rows.claim: Grammarians dislike an incomplete stop when a complete one is available; in the long jinn passage, stop at 72:18 if the following inna is kasra, but continue to 72:19 if it is fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب المستوفى النحويون يكرهون الوقف الناقص في التنزيل مع إمكان التام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An incomplete stop after ʿiwajan clarifies that qayyiman is separate and functions as a circumstantial accusative intended to precede it.
rows.anchor: كقوله ﴿ ولم يجعل له عوجا ﴾ فإن الوقف هنا يبين أن ﴿ قيما ﴾ منفصل عنه وأنه حال في نية التقديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stopping after “your nieces” marks the transition from prohibitions by blood relation to prohibitions by marriage or other cause.
rows.anchor: كقوله ﴿ وبنات الأخت ﴾ ليفصل به بين التحريم النسبي والسببي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some speech is composed to be heard with a pause, as the speaker’s lament over receiving his record continues into the next verse.
rows.anchor: نحو ﴿ يا ليتني لم أوت كتابيه ولم أدر ما حسابيه ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن الجزري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jazari says an otherwise permissible stop may be unsuitable in short clauses when a nearby stop gives a better break, even without grammatical attachment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الجزري وكما اغتفر الوقف لما ذكر قد لا يغتفر ولا يحسن فيما قصر من الجمل

rows.speaker: ابن الجزري
rows.claim: For parallelism, join a clause to its matching counterpart even when it could stand complete and has no grammatical link to what follows.
rows.anchor: وكذا يراعى في الوقف الازدواج فيوصل ما يوقف على نظيره مما يوجد التمام عليه

rows.speaker: ابن مردويه
rows.claim: In “the people told them,” the plural people denotes a single speaker: either Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud or a Bedouin from Khuzaʿa, who discouraged believers from meeting Abu Sufyan.
rows.anchor: والقائل واحد نعيم بن مسعود الأشجعي أو أعرابي من خزاعة كما أخرجه ابن مردويه

rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Farisi argues that the speaker is one person because the demonstrative is singular; a plural referent would call for “those” rather than “that.”
rows.anchor: قال الفارسي ومما يقوي أن المراد به واحد قوله ﴿ إنما ذلكم الشيطان ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “the people” means the Messenger, who gathered within himself the praiseworthy qualities found among people.
rows.anchor: أي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لجمعه ما في الناس من الخصال الحميدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets “the people” from whom they are to depart as Abraham.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن جرير من طريق الضحاك عن ابن عباس في قوله ﴿ من حيث أفاض الناس ﴾ قال إبراهيم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr has the unusual reading al-nāsī, “the forgetful,” instead of al-nās.
rows.anchor: ومن الغريب قراءة سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: المحتسب
rows.claim: Al-Muḥtasib takes al-nāsī to mean Adam, connecting it with the statement that Adam forgot and lacked resolve.
rows.anchor: قال في المحتسب يعني آدم لقوله ﴿ فنسي ولم نجد له عزما ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: In Ibn Masʿud’s reading, the angel who called to Zachariah is Gabriel.
rows.anchor: أي جبريل كما في قراءة ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples of general wording intended to denote a particular are numerous, and the category exceeds abrogated passages because every general wording has some specification.
rows.anchor: وأما المخصوص فأمثلته في القرآن كثيرة جدا وهو أكثر من المنسوخ إذ ما من عام إلا وقد خص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Connected specification includes exception, illustrated by passages that exclude repentant slanderers, believing poets, repentant wrongdoers, and other stated exceptions.
rows.anchor: ﴿ والشعراء يتبعهم الغاوون ﴾ إلى قوله ﴿ إلا الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Connected specification also occurs through a descriptive clause: the stepdaughters are specified as those in the husband’s household, from wives with whom he consummated marriage.
rows.anchor: الثاني الوصف نحو ﴿ وربائبكم اللاتي في حجوركم من نسائكم اللاتي دخلتم بهن ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Implicit meaning that agrees with the wording is either stronger (fahwā al-khiṭāb: forbidding striking parents) or equal (laḥn al-khiṭāb: forbidding destructive burning as well as eating an orphan’s wealth). Scholars dispute whether this inference is analogical or linguistic.
rows.anchor: فالأول ما يوافق حكمه المنطوق فإن كان أولى سمي فحوى الخطاب كدلالة ﴿ فلا تقل لهما أف ﴾ على تحريم الضرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contrary implication may arise from an adjective, circumstance, time, or number; examples infer no duty to verify a just reporter, no ban outside mosque retreat, no pilgrimage outside its stated months, and exactly eighty lashes.
rows.anchor: مفهوم صفة نعتا كان أو حالا أو ظرفا أو عددا نحو ﴿ إن جاءكم فاسق بنبأ فتبينوا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A condition can imply the absence of a ruling when it is absent: the command to support pregnant divorcees implies no such duty for those who are not pregnant.
rows.anchor: وشرط نحو ﴿ وإن كن أولات حمل فأنفقوا عليهن ﴾ أي فغير أولات الحمل لا يجب الإنفاق عليهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A stated endpoint implies the ruling changes after that endpoint, subject to its conditions: the first husband may remarry after she marries another husband.
rows.anchor: وغاية نحو ﴿ فلا تحل له من بعد حتى تنكح زوجا غيره ﴾ أي فإذا نكحته تحل للأول بشرطه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exclusive wording implies exclusion of all others: there is no god or guardian besides God, and worship is directed to God alone.
rows.anchor: وحصر نحو ﴿ لا إله إلا الله ﴾ ﴿ إنما إلهكم الله ﴾ أي فغيره ليس بإله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author regards these forms of implication as proof in principle, subject to conditions; most scholars reject an implication from stepdaughters being “in your houses” because that is the usual case.
rows.anchor: والأصح في الجملة أنها كلها حجة بشروط منها ألا يكون المذكور خرج للغالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For general wording used to praise or blame, one view keeps its full scope; another denies general scope because the purpose is praise or blame; the preferred view keeps it general absent a conflicting general text.
rows.anchor: فهل هو باق على عمومه فيه مذاهب أحدها نعم إذ لا صارف عنه ولا تنافي بين العموم وبين المدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chastity passage shows praise-language can remain general when no contrary text conflicts with it.
rows.anchor: مثاله ولا معارض قوله تعالى ﴿ إن الأبرار لفي نعيم وإن الفجار لفي جحيم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a praise passage might seem to permit combining two sisters through ownership, the non-praise prohibition against combining sisters limits that general reading.
rows.anchor: فإنه سيق للمدح وظاهره يعم الأختين بملك اليمين جمعا وعارضه في ذلك ﴿ وأن تجمعوا بين الأختين ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A warning against hoarding appears to include lawful jewelry, but Jabir’s report that jewelry bears no zakat restricts the general wording.
rows.anchor: ومثاله في الذم ﴿ والذين يكنزون الذهب والفضة ﴾ الآية فإنه سيق للذم وظاهره يعم الحلي المباح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether a command addressed specifically to the Prophet covers the community is disputed; the preferred legal-theory view says no, because the wording singles him out.
rows.anchor: اختلف في الخطاب الخاص به صلى الله عليه وسلم نحو ﴿ يا أيها النبي ﴾ ﴿ يا أيها الرسول ﴾ هل يشمل الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars hold that a general address to people includes the Prophet because the wording is general; al-Zuhri reports that he is among the believers addressed by commands to believe.
rows.anchor: على مذاهب أصحها وعليه الأكثرون نعم لعموم الصيغة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views exclude the Prophet because the message is spoken through him for others, or exclude him only when the address is preceded by “say,” while including him otherwise.
rows.anchor: والثاني لا لأنه ورد على لسانه لتبليغ غيره ولما له من الخصائص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred legal-theory view is that “O people” includes unbelievers and enslaved people because its wording is general.
rows.anchor: الرابع الأصح في الأصول أن الخطاب ( يأيها الناس ) يشمل الكافر والعبد لعموم اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sufficient stop is detached in wording but connected in meaning, allowing a pause and restart; “your mothers are forbidden” is such a stop.
rows.anchor: والكافي منقطع في اللفظ متعلق في المعنى فيحسن الوقف عليه والابتداء بما بعده أيضا نحو ﴿ حرمت عليكم أمهاتكم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A good stop may be made, but starting with the words that follow is not sound; the opening praise is the example.
rows.anchor: والحسن هو الذي يحسن الوقف عليه ولا يحسن الابتداء بما بعده نحو ﴿ الحمد لله رب العالمين ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A repugnant stop leaves the intended meaning unclear; stopping at “those who said have disbelieved” and restarting with “God is the Messiah” creates an impossible meaning, and doing so deliberately with that intent is unbelief.
rows.anchor: وأقبح منه الوقف على ﴿ لقد كفر الذين قالوا ﴾ ويبتدئ ﴿ إن الله هو المسيح ﴾ لأن المعنى مستحيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worst stop cuts off a negation before its affirmation; if breath forces it, the reciter may pause but should return to connect the phrase.
rows.anchor: وأقبح من هذا الوقف على المنفي دون حرف الإيجاب نحو ﴿ لا إله إلا الله ﴾

rows.speaker: السجاوندي
rows.claim: Al-Sajawandi classifies pauses into five ranks: necessary, unrestricted, permissible, permitted for a reason, and licensed by necessity.
rows.anchor: وقال السجاوندي الوقف على خمس مراتب لازم ومطلق وجائز ومجوز لوجه ومرخص ضرورة

rows.speaker: السجاوندي
rows.claim: A necessary stop prevents the next clause from being misread as describing believers; the intended passage denies belief and then affirms their deception.
rows.anchor: فاللازم ما لو وصل طرفاه غير المراد نحو قوله ﴿ وما هم بمؤمنين ﴾ يلزم الوقف هنا

rows.speaker: السجاوندي
rows.claim: A necessary stop also separates “not tamed” from “plowing the earth,” preventing the second clause from falling within the first negation.
rows.anchor: وكما في قوله ﴿ لا ذلول تثير الأرض ﴾ فإن جملة تثير صفة ل ذلول داخلة حيز النفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural wording paired with plural wording can distribute to each individual: “your mothers” means each addressee’s own mother; likewise each has his own children and each mother nurses her own child.
rows.anchor: مقابلة الجمع بالجمع تارة تقتضي مقابلة كل فرد من هذا بكل فرد من هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural-to-plural wording can also assign the whole stated plural amount to every person judged, so each slanderer receives eighty lashes; Ibn ʿIzz al-Din applies the pattern to each believer’s gardens.
rows.anchor: وتارة يقتضي ثبوت الجمع لكل فرد من أفراد المحكوم عليه نحو ﴿ فاجلدوهم ثمانين جلدة ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sometimes plural-to-plural wording can support either distribution, so contextual evidence must determine which reading applies.
rows.anchor: وتارة يحتمل الأمرين فيحتاج إلى دليل يعين أحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural subjects paired with a singular object usually do not distribute universally, but here each person owes a meal for one poor person for each day; the lashes command likewise applies to each slanderer.
rows.anchor: وأما مقابل الجمع بالمفرد فالغالب ألا يقتضي تعميم المفرد وقد يقتضيه

rows.speaker: جلال الدين البلقيني
rows.claim: Al-Bulqini calls a general wording that remains fully universal rare, since one can imagine a specification for almost every general text; he illustrates with several legal examples.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي جلال الدين البلقيني ومثاله عزيز إذ مامن عام إلا ويتخيل فيه التخصيص

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashi says fully general wording is frequent in the Qurʾan and cites divine knowledge and justice, creation, and the earth as examples.
rows.anchor: وذكر الزركشي في البرهان أنه كثير في القرآن وأورد منه ﴿ وأن الله بكل شيء عليم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author limits al-Bulqini’s claim of rarity to subsidiary legal rulings and identifies the prohibition of close female relatives as a legal generality without exception.
rows.anchor: قلت هذه الآيات كلها في غير الأحكام الفرعية فالظاهر أن مراد البلقيني أنه عزيز في الأحكام الفرعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A general phrase intended specifically was never meant to cover every member; a specified general phrase was meant to cover them linguistically, though not all remain under its legal ruling.
rows.anchor: أن الأول لم يرد شموله لجميع الأفراد لا من جهة تناول اللفظ ولا من جهة الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first category is metaphorical by agreement; the second is disputed but the author prefers that it remains literal, as most Shafiʿis, many Hanafis, and all Hanbalis hold.
rows.anchor: ومنها أن الأول مجاز قطعا لنقل اللفظ عن موضوعه الأصلي بخلاف الثاني فإن فيه مذاهب أصحها أنه حقيقة

rows.speaker: أبو حامد
rows.claim: Abu Hamid attributes the literal reading of the specified general to al-Shafiʿi and his followers; al-Subki approves because the word’s reach to the remainder is genuinely literal.
rows.anchor: وقال الشيخ أبو حامد إنه مذهب الشافعي وأصحابه وصححه السبكي لأن تناول اللفظ للبعض الباقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The categories also differ in their indicators: the first has a rational indicator that cannot be separated, and may refer to one member by agreement; the second has a textual indicator that can disappear, and its singular reading is disputed.
rows.anchor: ومنها أن قرينة الأول عقلية والثاني لفظيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some consider the theft ruling ambiguous because hand can mean the wrist, elbow, or shoulder and cutting can mean amputation or wounding; the Prophet’s cutting at the wrist clarifies it.
rows.anchor: منها آية السرقة قيل إنها مجملة في اليد لأنها تطلق على العضو إلى الكوع وإلى المرفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others deny ambiguity in the theft verse, arguing that “cutting” clearly means amputation.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا إجمال فيها لأن القطع ظاهر في الإبانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read “wipe your heads” as ambiguous between wiping all the head and part of it, with the Prophet’s wiping the forelock clarifying the intended extent.
rows.anchor: ومنها ﴿ وامسحوا برؤوسكم ﴾ قيل إنها مجملة لترددها بين مسح الكل والبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others say the wording simply requires an act called wiping, which is satisfied by the minimum amount bearing that name.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا وإنما هي لمطلق المسح الصادق بأقل ما يطلق عليه الاسم ويفيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view treats “your mothers are forbidden” as ambiguous because prohibition attaches to an act, not a person, and the omitted act could be supplied in several ways.
rows.anchor: قيل مجملة لأن إسناد التحريم إلى العين لا يصح لأن إنما يتعلق بالفعل فلا بد من تقديره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opposing view says ordinary usage resolves the ellipsis: the prohibition means sexual enjoyment through intercourse or similar acts, as with other rulings attached to persons.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا لوجود المرجح وهو العرف فإنه يقضي بأن المراد تحريم الاستمتاع بوطء أو نحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view calls the sale and usury verse ambiguous because every sale contains an increase and clarification is needed to identify lawful and unlawful increases.
rows.anchor: قيل إنها مجملة لأن الربا الزيادة وما من بيع إلا وفيه زيادة

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi reports that al-Shafiʿi’s soundest view treats the sale wording as general: all sales are permitted except those specified by evidence, since the Prophet forbade familiar sales without listing all lawful ones.
rows.anchor: وقال الماوردي للشافعي في هذه الآية أربعة أقوال أحدها أنها عامة فإن لفظها لفظ عموم

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi distinguishes a general phrase intended generally, though later specified, from a general phrase intended particularly, whose specification is explained before the wording is uttered.
rows.anchor: قال فعلى هذا في العموم قولان أحدهما أنه عموم أريد به العموم وإن دخله التخصيص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording leaves out distinctions supplied by context: wait until menstrual blood ceases, then until the woman washes; only after both forms of purification may the husband approach.
rows.anchor: أي حتى يطهرن من الدم ويتطهرن بالماء فإذا طهرن وتطهرن فأتوهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The compact wording implies that they mixed a good deed with a bad one, and another bad deed with a good one.
rows.anchor: أي عملا صالحا بسيئ وآخر سيئا صالح

words: فِئَةٌ تُقَٰتِلُ فِى سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَأُخْرَىٰ كَافِرَةٌ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence omits that one group is believing and fights for God, while the other is unbelieving and fights for falsehood.
rows.anchor: قلت ومن لطيفه قوله ﴿ فئة تقاتل في سبيل الله وأخرى كافرة ﴾

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani reconstructs reciprocal omissions from the two sides of a comparison; each side supplies what was omitted from the other, making this an especially eloquent construction.
rows.anchor: وفي الغرائب للكرماني في الآية الأولى التقدير ( مثل الذين كفروا معك يا محمد كمثل الناعق مع الغنم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term ḥabk evokes tightly woven cloth: a discerning reader fills the omissions in their proper places, closing gaps in the meaning while giving it beauty and polish.
rows.anchor: ومأخذ هذه التسمية من الحبك الذي معناه الشد والأحكام وتحسين أثر الصنعة في الثوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth deletion type, ikhtizal, covers omissions outside earlier types, including omitted nouns, verbs, particles, or multiple elements.
rows.anchor: النوع الرابع ما يسمى بالاختزال هو ما ليس واحدا مما سبق وهو أقسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A common omitted noun is the genitive complement: “your mothers are forbidden” means marriage to your mothers; Ibn Jinni estimates nearly a thousand such cases in the Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: حذف المضاف هو كثير في القرآن جدا حتى قال ابن جني في القرآن منه زهاء ألف موضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other omitted complements yield “pilgrimage in months” or “the months of pilgrimage”; “righteousness” denotes a righteous person or the person’s righteousness.
rows.anchor: ومنه ﴿ الحج أشهر ﴾ أي حج أشهر أو أشهر الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “double in life and double in death,” the omitted complement is punishment; “in the necks” means freeing enslaved people.
rows.anchor: ﴿ لأذقناك ضعف الحياة وضعف الممات ﴾ أي ضعف عذاب ﴿ وفي الرقاب ﴾ أي وفي تحرير الرقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive complement is often omitted from the first-person yāʾ suffix, as in “my Lord, forgive me.”
rows.anchor: حذف المضاف إليه يكثر في ياء المتكلم نحو ﴿ رب اغفر لي ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that eight verses in al-Nisaʾ are better for this community than what the sun rises and sets upon; the list begins with God’s guidance, repentance, and the relief of 4:28.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال ثماني آيات نزلت في سورة النساء هن خير لهذه الأمة مما طلعت عليه الشمس وغربت

words: إِنَّ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا رَبُّنَا اللَّهُ ثُمَّ اسْتَقَٰمُوا
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Asked which verse is most hopeful, Ibn Abbas answers with the verse about those who profess God as Lord and then remain steadfast.
rows.anchor: سئل ابن عباس أي آية أرجى في كتاب الله

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A man tells Umar that the most severe verse is the promise that whoever does evil will be repaid; Umar says its revelation once made them fear that no food or drink would help, until the later forgiveness verse brought relief.
rows.anchor: قال ﴿ من يعمل سوءا يجز به ﴾ فما منا أحد يعمل سوءا إلا جزي به فقال عمر لبثنا حين نزلت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says Abu Barza al-Aslami identified the warning that the people of Hell will receive only more punishment as the harshest verse for them.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن الحسن قال سألت أبا برزة الأسلمي عن أشد آية في كتاب الله

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan says, in al-Bukhari’s Ṣaḥīḥ, that the verse requiring the People of the Book to uphold the Torah, Gospel, and revelation is the most severe verse for him.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح البخاري عن سفيان قال ما في القرآن آية أشد علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To interpret the Qurʾan, first explain its general or condensed passages from other Qurʾanic passages where they are expanded; Ibn al-Jawzi wrote a book on such cross-explanations.
rows.anchor: طلبه أولا من القرآن فما أجمل منه في مكان فقد فسر في موضع آخر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: If the Qurʾan does not settle the point, consult the Sunna, which explains it; al-Shafiʿi says every ruling the Messenger made came from what God showed him in the Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: فإن أعياه ذلك طلبه من السنة فإنها شارحة للقرآن وموضحة له وقد قال الشافعي

rows.speaker: الحاكم
rows.claim: When the Qurʾan and Sunna do not settle the interpretation, consult the Companions, who witnessed the circumstances of revelation; al-Hakim says a Companion’s tafsir from an eyewitness has the status of a Prophetic report.
rows.anchor: فإن لم يجده في السنة رجع إلى أقوال الصحابة فإنهم أدرى بذلك لما شاهدوه من القرائن

rows.speaker: أبو طالب الطبري
rows.claim: Abu Talib al-Tabari requires a sound creed and adherence to the Sunna, warning that religiously suspect or partisan interpreters may mislead people away from the Salaf and the path of guidance.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن من شرطه صحة الاعتقاد أولا ولزوم سنة الدين فإن من كان مغموصا عليه في دينه

rows.speaker: أبو طالب الطبري
rows.claim: The interpreter should rely on transmitted material from the Prophet, Companions, and their contemporaries and avoid innovations; reconcile differing Companion explanations when possible, since they may express one underlying meaning.
rows.anchor: ويجب أن يكون اعتماده على النقل عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وعن أصحابه ومن عاصرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says the Qurʾan came in portions to preserve it in the heart of the unlettered Prophet, who could not read or write, unlike literate earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: وقيل معنى ﴿ لنثبت به فؤادك ﴾ أي لنحفظه فإنه عليه السلام كان أميا لا يقرأ ولا يكتب

rows.speaker: ابن فورك
rows.claim: Ibn Furak explains that the Torah descended as a whole to the literate Moses, while the Qurʾan descended piecemeal because it was sent unwritten to an unlettered Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن فورك قيل أنزلت التوراة جملة لأنها نزلت على نبي يكتب ويقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that gradual revelation permits abrogation and responds to questions and objections as they arise; Ibn Abbas says Gabriel brought answers to people’s words and deeds, explaining the verse about answering their examples with truth.
rows.anchor: إنما لم ينزل جملة واحدة لأن منه الناسخ والمنسوخ ولا يتأتى ذلك إلا فيما أنزل مفرقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Fulfill the covenants” encompasses everything the Qurʾan makes lawful, unlawful, obligatory, or defined.
rows.anchor: ﴿ أوفوا بالعقود ﴾ ما أحل وما حرم وما فرض وما حد في القرآن كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yajrimannakum means “impel you.”
rows.anchor: 1576 ﴿ يجرمنكم ﴾ يحملنكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaʾnān means enmity.
rows.anchor: 1577 ﴿ شنآن ﴾ عداوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Birr means what God commands, while taqwa means what God forbids.
rows.anchor: ﴿ على البر والتقوى ﴾ البر ما أمرت به والتقوى ما نهيت عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-munkhaniqa is an animal strangled to death.
rows.anchor: 1579 ﴿ والمنخنقة ﴾ التي تخنق فتموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mawqudha is an animal beaten to death with wood.
rows.anchor: ﴿ والموقوذة ﴾ التي تضرب بالخشب فتموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mutaraddiya is an animal that falls from a mountain.
rows.anchor: ﴿ والمتردية ﴾ التي تتردى من الجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-natiha is a sheep gored by another sheep.
rows.anchor: ﴿ والنطيحة ﴾ الشاة التي تنطح الشاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What a predatory beast has eaten means what it has seized.
rows.anchor: ﴿ وما أكل السبع ﴾ ما أخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means an animal you slaughter while it still has life.
rows.anchor: ﴿ إلا ما ذكيتم ﴾ ذبحتم وبه روح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-azlam are divining arrows.
rows.anchor: 1585 ﴿ بالأزلام ﴾ القداح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayra mutajanif means not leaning toward or committing sin.
rows.anchor: 1586 ﴿ غير متجانف ﴾ متعد لإثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-jawarih includes dogs, cheetahs, falcons, and similar hunting animals.
rows.anchor: ﴿ من الجوارح ﴾ الكلاب والفهود والصقور وأشباهها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukallibin means trained, hunting animals.
rows.anchor: 1588 ﴿ مكلبين ﴾ ضواري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food of the People of the Book means their slaughtered animals.
rows.anchor: وطعام الذين أوتوا الكتاب ﴾ ذبائحهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Moses’ prayer, ifruq means “separate” or “decide between us.”
rows.anchor: 1590 ﴿ فافرق ﴾ فافصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fitna in the phrase about one whom God wills to test means misguidance.
rows.anchor: 1591 ﴿ ومن يرد الله فتنته ﴾ ضلالته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhaymin means trustworthy: the Qurʾan is trusted over every earlier scripture.
rows.anchor: ﴿ ومهيمنا عليه ﴾ أمينا القرآن أمين على كل كتاب قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shirʿa and minhaj mean a path and a practice.
rows.anchor: 1593 ﴿ شرعة ومنهاجا ﴾ سبيلا وسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adhilla ʿala al-muʾminin means merciful toward the believers.
rows.anchor: 1594 ﴿ أذلة على المؤمنين ﴾ رحماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A hand bound” is what the Jews call God, accusing Him of withholding; God is exalted above that.
rows.anchor: ﴿ مغلولة ﴾ يعنون بخيل أمسك ما عنده تعالى الله عن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A bahira was a she-camel whose fifth offspring, if male, was slaughtered for men to eat, while women were excluded.
rows.anchor: ﴿ بحيرة ﴾ هي الناقة إذا أنتجت خمسة أبطن نظروا إلى الخامس فإن كان ذكرا ذبحوه فأكله الرجال دون النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the fifth offspring was female, the camel’s ears were slit as part of the taboo custom.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت أنثى جدعوا أذنيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saʾiba was livestock dedicated to idols, from which people would not ride, milk, shear wool, or carry anything.
rows.anchor: وأما السائبة فكانوا يسيبون من أنعامهم لآلهتهم لا يركبون لها ظهرا ولا يحلبون لها لبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a wasila sheep’s seventh birth, a dead lamb, whether male or female, was shared by men and women.
rows.anchor: وأما الوصيلة فالشاة إذا نتجت سبعة أبطن نظروا السابع فإن كان ذكرا أو أنثى وهو ميت اشترك فيه الرجال والنساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a male and female were twins, they spared the female and claimed her brother had joined her, making her forbidden to them.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت أنثى وذكرا في بطن استحيوها وقالوا وصلته أخته فحرمته علينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ham was a male camel whose offspring had themselves reproduced; people then protected his back and wool and did not bar him from pasture or water.
rows.anchor: وأما الحام فالفحل من الإبل إذا ولد لولده قالوا حمى هذا ظهره فلا يحملون عليه شيئا
